answers.text: Histamine 2 receptor antagonists work on a specific cell called the parietal cell that is located in gastric pits of the lining of the stomach.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While it is true that some of the Histamine 2 receptor blockers are exposed to the parietal cells, that portion of the parietal cell is not the portion that has the Histamine 2 receptor. The drug must be absorbed in order for it to access the cell 'from the other way'
tipsAndFeedback.notChosenFeedback: Indeed, while it is true that some of the Histamine 2 receptor blockers are exposed to the parietal cells, that portion of the parietal cell is not the portion that has the Histamine 2 receptor. The drug must be absorbed in order for it to access the cell 'from the other way'

answers.text: Histamine 2 receptor antagonists affect the parietal cell directly, without having to be absorbed, because the medication is exposed to those cells when it is in the stomach.

The parietal cells have a trans-membrane protein carrier called a hydrogen potassium ATPase pump that secrete the H+ (sometimes called protons; sometimes called ‘acid’) into the gastric pits and on to the stomach, but need three things to bind to the cell at the same time in order for that to occur, Histamine 2, Acetylcholine (from the parasympathetic rest and digest system) and gastrin (Gastrin is a hormone that is released when there are peptides in the stomach.).

answers.text: The Histamine 2 receptor blockers like Famotidine and other ….tidine drugs are competitive antagonists, so they compete with the Histamine 2 that is in the area of the parietal cell. There is still some Histamine 2 binding in the parietal cell and still some acid being secreted, so it will never be 100% effective,
